regions.label: abstract
regions.text: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud–edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

For real-time interaction, a cloud–edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

Agents must continually make strategic decisions and manage resources under partial observability and delayed feedback, all through fine-grained, low-level keyboard and mouse actions. Tasks may last hours or longer, requiring reliable memory, planning, and decision-making throughout. Such environments therefore serve as an uncompromising benchmark for coordinating perception, reasoning, memory, and control.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Honkai: Star Rail (HSR) exemplifies this setting by condensing these demands into a continuously evolving game environment. Its gameplay combines narrative-driven exploration across diverse regions with turn-based combat, squad management, resource allocation, and multi-level UI operation. This environment features nested objectives and long-term progression that challenge an agent’s cross-task generalization, long-term memory, and closed-loop execution. Developing agents in this system compels MLLMs to transition from passive visual understanding to sustained, proactive interaction. Mastering such challenges paves a concrete pathway toward generalist agents capable of operating across both complex digital worlds and embodied physical environments. As illustrated in Figure 1 , Gamer is designed to operate across visually and mechanically diverse environments via a single screen-to-action interface.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Although games have long served as standard testbeds for AI, extending these successes to modern, complex games remains challenging. With domain-specific policy optimization, prior agents have matched or exceeded human performance in benchmarks such as Atari [ 31 ], Minecraft [ 12 ], and StarCraft [ 47 ]. However, these methods typically use privileged internal states, tailored action spaces, or dedicated APIs, which generalize poorly beyond their narrow training domains. As summarized in Table 1 , existing game agents differ substantially in their training recipes, game coverage, and real-time execution capabilities. Because modern games rarely expose internal states or dedicated interaction APIs, a true generalist agent should operate like a human player [ 37 , 45 , 55 ]: perceiving the world through raw visual pixels and acting through standard keyboard-and-mouse interfaces. Unifying transferable control, long-horizon decision-making, and non-invasive execution within a single generalist model remains largely unaddressed.

regions.text: To address these challenges, we present Gamer, a scalable generalist agent framework for complex interactive games. Gamer observes raw screen pixels and executes native keyboard and mouse controls. This unified device-level interface enables non-invasive interaction across diverse environments, eliminating reliance on game-specific APIs or customized action spaces. We first conduct continued pre-training (CPT) on thousands of hours of multi-source gameplay trajectories and map heterogeneous control formats into a unified keyboard and-mouse representation to establish a transferable control prior. A scalable data-construction pipeline is built to transform raw gameplay trajectories into multi-level instruction data. Using LLM-assisted annotation, the pipeline adds task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and memory summaries while preserving the original observation-action sequences. We produce over a thousand hours of instruction data covering local operations, intermediate subgoals, and complete tasks. We leverage this corpus for sparse-thinking instruction tuning, enabling the policy to organize executable behavior around long-horizon objectives while retaining task-relevant memory. Finally, we introduce Temporal-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (TA-GRPO)

regions.label: text
regions.text: To address these challenges, we present Gamer, a scalable generalist agent framework for complex interactive games. Gamer observes raw screen pixels and executes native keyboard and mouse controls. This unified device-level interface enables non-invasive interaction across diverse environments, eliminating reliance on game-specific APIs or customized action spaces. We first conduct continued pre-training (CPT) on thousands of hours of multi-source gameplay trajectories and map heterogeneous control formats into a unified keyboard and-mouse representation to establish a transferable control prior. A scalable data-construction pipeline is built to transform raw gameplay trajectories into multi-level instruction data. Using LLM-assisted annotation, the pipeline adds task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and memory summaries while preserving the original observation-action sequences. We produce over a thousand hours of instruction data covering local operations, intermediate subgoals, and complete tasks. We leverage this corpus for sparse-thinking instruction tuning, enabling the policy to organize executable behavior around long-horizon objectives while retaining task-relevant memory. Finally, we introduce Temporal-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (TA-GRPO) to further optimize the game policy through online environment feedback and address accumulated execution errors and sparse rewards over extended interactions. We support large-scale training and real-time deployment through a unified training, evaluation, and inference infrastructure. We extend Verl [ 44 ] to support CPT, SFT, and online RL within a shared training framework, with self-developed Streaming-vLLM serving as the inference engine for interactive evaluation and rollout generation. Streaming-vLLM combines stateful KV-cache reuse, architecture-aware execution, FSM-guided speculative decoding with BF16 verification, and streaming action dispatch to reduce inference latency. Equipped with a sandbox supporting concurrent game instances and a data pipeline that collects trajectories and identifies failures, this system enables iterative policy improvement under real-time interaction constraints. Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled human players on several challenging 3D game tasks and achieves competitive performance on a range of traditional 2D game benchmarks in real-time. These results demonstrate that a unified keyboard-and-mouse action space which is coupled with cross-domain trajectory scaling and real-time online learning can offer a viable pathway toward generalist interactive agents.

Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled human players on several challenging 3D game tasks and achieves competitive performance on a range of traditional 2D game benchmarks in real-time. These results demonstrate that a unified keyboard-and-mouse action space which is coupled with cross-domain trajectory scaling and real-time online learning can offer a viable pathway toward generalist interactive agents.

regions.text: • A scalable pipeline for long-horizon instruction data construction. We develop a pipeline that transforms multi-source and multi-format gameplay trajectories into instruction data. Through LLM-assisted annotation and quality validation, the pipeline enriches recorded interactions with task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and persistent memory summaries. Applied to tens of thousands of hours of gameplay data, it produces over a thousand hours of high-quality instruction data spanning operations, subgoals, and complete quests, providing supervision for long-horizon reasoning and control.

regions.text: Games differ in world, mechanics, and objectives, but most games share a unified device-level interface: screen observations and native keyboard and mouse inputs. As shown in Figure 2 , CPT adapts a pretrained multimodal model to this interface and learns transferable control from trajectories collected across environments. We first unify action representations across games and reduce biases caused by key frequencies and repeated control states. We then summarize findings from GameScaling [ 62 ] on how model capacity, gameplay data, and game composition affect control learning and cross-game generalization.

regions.text: where ∆ P t is the accumulated mouse movement in the interval t , and t,j ( j = 1 , . . . , 6 ) is the set of keyboard K keys and mouse buttons pressed in action block j . We show more details of the action format in Figure 3 . Each block lasts approximately 33 ms, yielding a 30 Hz action rate. Keys and buttons shared by consecutive blocks remain pressed, while those absent from the next block are released. This representation supports held movement, brief taps, dragging, and simultaneous input combinations without increasing the visual observation rate. Actions are serialized using the pretrained language model’s output vocabulary, without an additional output head.

Uneven key frequencies encourage the model to associate actions with specific inputs rather than their functions, while long runs of repeated actions can dominate the token-level supervision. We address these biases with random key remapping and repeat-aware loss decay, respectively.

regions.label: text
regions.text: CPT learns transferable action control from visual observations, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches the model to follow explicit task objectives. We train on tasks at different difficulty levels, from local operations and intermediate subgoals to complete objectives, with reasoning and memory summaries at key decision points. The need for reasoning is inherently sparse in long-horizon gameplay. Routine movement and repeated attacks favor direct action, while route failures, target switches, and resource decisions often require replanning. Gamer therefore uses a single autoregressive policy to alternate between direct control, sparse reasoning, and memory updates. Persistent summaries carry task state across context boundaries. Figure 4 illustrates how adaptive reasoning and memory compaction are integrated into an interaction sequence.

At routine control steps, the model sets r t = ∅ and generates an action directly. At decision-critical or memory-update steps, the model generates reasoning before the action. Current reasoning captures immediate judgment, next subgoal, or short-term plan, such as revising a route, selecting an interaction target, or switching combat strategy. Memory summaries, by contrast, retain information needed beyond the current context, including task progress, important locations, resource states, failed attempts, and remaining plans. The policy learns when to generate reasoning within the same autoregressive process, without a separate classifier or routing head. Here, r t refers only to the explicitly supervised reasoning text generated by the policy and does not characterize all latent computation within the model.

regions.label: text
regions.text: CPT and SFT provide cross-game control and task-following capabilities, while online RL improves the policy on states encountered during its own interactions. Online RL in real-time games faces two challenges: long interactions can exceed the model’s context window, and delayed model responses can change the environment transitions observed during rollout collection. We address the first using Temporal-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO) and the second using the shared Streaming-vLLM infrastructure (Sec. 5 ). Together, they enable policy optimization over long sequences of real-time keyboard and mouse interaction.

regions.label: text
regions.text: As illustrated in Figure 5 , TA-GRPO divides long rollouts into finite segments linked by the same memory compaction mechanism used during SFT. It scores segments from separate rollouts of the same task using verifiable outcomes and assigns group-relative advantages [ 43 ] to the decisions within each segment. The policy can therefore learn from long interactions without fitting a full trajectory into one context or repeatedly restoring an intermediate game state. The policy retains the same input and output format, generating reasoning, memory updates, and executable actions as needed.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Real-time gameplay introduces timing constraints that are absent when evaluation pauses the game during inference. The results in Sec. 8.2 show that a policy can perform well in a paused game but degrade sharply when the game state changes before its actions arrive. This temporal mismatch also affects online policy optimization: delayed actions change subsequent states and the verified feedback in collected trajectories. At the same time, long-horizon training requires many independent environments to advance concurrently.

regions.label: text
regions.text: We develop Streaming-vLLM as a common execution backend for training, evaluation, and deployment. The backend retains KV states across turns under memory compaction and reduces model execution cost. It also verifies structural tokens proposed by a fast finite-state machine (FSM) and streams verified action blocks before the full packet is complete. The model-facing interface is shared across Qwen3-VL [ 3 ] and Qwen3.5 [ 40 ], including dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones. Architecture-specific kernels and schedules support each backbone while preserving the same observation–action protocol. Appendix C reports representative Dense and MoE serving configurations on Ampere (NVIDIA A800) and Hopper (NVIDIA H200).

regions.label: figure_title
regions.title: Figure 6 Streaming-vLLM for persistent multi-environment inference. Each game client maintains separate short-term history, long-term memory, and logical KV-cache state. Two cache forms coexist. Full-Attention layers keep a growing paged KV cache: blocks are allocated and reused on demand, and released when context is compacted. In hybrid backbones, gated delta network (GDN) layers instead hold fixed-size linear recurrent and convolution states ( ssm_state , conv_state ) whose footprint is independent of sequence length and which are carried across compaction in place. Paged allocation and memory-aware KV-cache reuse avoid repeated context processing, while incremental rotary position embedding (RoPE) refresh corrects retained keys after compaction. The runtime combines architecture-aware execution, BF16-verified FSM speculation, and early action dispatch to serve concurrent real-time interactions.

regions.text: At each interaction step, the model consumes the control specification, task instruction, long-term memory, and recent observation-action history ( , I, t , t ) . Re-encoding the visual and textual history at every turn B M H would repeat the same prefill work. As shown in Figure 6 , Streaming-vLLM instead preserves KV states of retained context and computes new states only for newly appended tokens, following stateful streaming inference [ 57 , 58 ]. A short-term queue holds recent complete interaction rounds, while a long-term queue stores generated memory summaries. At a compaction boundary, the policy summarizes history before eviction. The discarded rounds release their KV pages, and recent rounds retain cached states. Each environment keeps its own logical-to-physical block table over the paged allocator [ 17 ], allowing requests with different history lengths to coexist.

regions.text: Compaction also changes the logical token positions of retained states. regions.label: text
regions.text: Frequent short requests incur costs beyond prefill, including decoder launches, inter-device communication, and architecture-specific operations. Streaming-vLLM separates a common serving interface from specialized execution paths. Dense and MoE variants share action serialization, context compaction, and client scheduling, while the compute backend accommodates their respective attention, expert, and recurrent or gated-delta network operations. We combine operator fusion, tensor-parallel execution, communication overlap, and CUDA Graph replay to reduce serial overhead. We apply tensor parallelism selectively. It can reduce decoder compute time, but communication and synchronization may outweigh the savings for the smaller ViT workload. The measured tradeoff is analyzed in Table 9 . Across Ampere and Hopper GPUs, decode and speculative verification are each implemented as an all-layer megakernel that combines fine-grained L2 prefetching, in-place cross-rank reduction and normalization, and a fused sampling and state-machine tail to minimize CPU and synchronization overhead. For vision encoding and context prefill, persistent kernels overlap tile-level communication with computation and fold cross-rank reduction and normalization into the GEMM epilogue. Finally, W8A8 quantization yields only modest end-to-end gains and is applied selectively: ViT remains in BF16 to avoid low-precision representation instability, prefill quantizes only large QKV and MoE expert projections to prevent router flips and GDN state drift across short single-frame extensions, and low-batch decode is latency- and barrier-bound rather than compute-bound.

For vision encoding and context prefill, persistent kernels overlap tile-level communication with computation and fold cross-rank reduction and normalization into the GEMM epilogue. Dense and MoE variants share action serialization, context compaction, and client scheduling, while the compute backend accommodates their respective attention, expert, and recurrent or gated-delta network operations. We combine operator fusion, tensor-parallel execution, communication overlap, and CUDA Graph replay to reduce serial overhead. We apply tensor parallelism selectively. It can reduce decoder compute time, but communication and synchronization may outweigh the savings for the smaller ViT workload. The measured tradeoff is analyzed in Table 9 . Across Ampere and Hopper GPUs, decode and speculative verification are each implemented as an all-layer megakernel that combines fine-grained L2 prefetching, in-place cross-rank reduction and normalization, and a fused sampling and state-machine tail to minimize CPU and synchronization overhead. regions.text: 5.3 Verified FSM Decoding and Streaming Actions After execution overhead is reduced, autoregressive generation remains sequential. A fast finite-state-machine (FSM) drafter proposes predictable structural tokens in the reasoning–action output. The FSM tracks <think> , </think> , <|action_start|> , and <|action_end|> boundaries. It proposes closing an empty reasoning span or starting an action packet after reasoning ends. Within the action, it drafts whitespace after mouse-coordinate numbers, the separator following the Z coordinate, and predictable delimiters and empty-key patterns across the six keyboard-mouse groups. Mouse-coordinate values remain model-generated. During generation, the FSM enforces constrained sampling over valid transitions via state-dependent vocabulary bitmasks at every decoding and verification position, while simultaneously packing candidate continuations from the next grammar states into a draft tree that the target model verifies through a single shared-prefix pass [ 6 , 18 , 21 , 30 , 67 ], committing only accepted prefixes. The policy retains control over action selection, while verification reduces the number of sequential decoding iterations. See Appendix C.1 for more details. Streaming-vLLM also reduces the time to the first executable action. Once the mouse fields and first verified key block are ready, the server sends that prefix to the client while the remaining blocks continue decoding. The client executes the six blocks in order, maintaining key press-hold-release semantics. Action execution can therefore begin while the remaining blocks are still being generated. A fast finite-state-machine (FSM) drafter proposes predictable structural tokens in the reasoning–action output. The FSM tracks <think> , </think> , <|action_start|> , and <|action_end|> boundaries. It proposes closing an empty reasoning span or starting an action packet after reasoning ends. Within the action, it drafts whitespace after mouse-coordinate numbers, the separator following the Z coordinate, and predictable delimiters and empty-key patterns across the six keyboard-mouse groups. Mouse-coordinate values remain model-generated. During generation, the FSM enforces constrained sampling over valid transitions via state-dependent vocabulary bitmasks at every decoding and verification position, while simultaneously packing candidate continuations from the next grammar states into a draft tree that the target model verifies through a single shared-prefix pass [ 6 , 18 , 21 , 30 , 67 ], committing only accepted prefixes. The policy retains control over action selection, while verification reduces the number of sequential decoding iterations. See Appendix C.1 for more details.

regions.text: Real-time rollouts require scheduling that accounts for both action deadlines and throughput. Each active environment is assigned an isolated resident state slot that holds its short-term history, long-term memory,

regions.label: text
regions.text: Real-time rollouts require scheduling that accounts for both action deadlines and throughput. Each active environment is assigned an isolated resident state slot that holds its short-term history, long-term memory, and model states, avoiding context rebuilds when environments alternate turns. The runtime time-division multiplexes incoming frames’ vision encoding and context extension across slots over a shared workspace, and then performs batched token generation and verification across all ready environments. Within each slot, paged KV caches and linear recurrent (GDN) states follow different update rules during scheduling: KV caches are position-indexed, so speculative tokens write directly to trailing slots and rejected suffixes are simply overwritten on the next step, whereas fixed-size recurrent states update in place and are committed only for the accepted prefix after verification. This balances aggregate throughput against the progress rate of each active environment. Real-time evaluation and TA-GRPO training share the same serving path, so training rollouts are collected under the same execution protocol while the game continues to advance.

Section 8.6 reports latency and closed-loop evaluations, and Appendix C.4 provides representative GPU, precision, and parallelism settings.

regions.text: Raw gameplay videos provide rich visual and control experience, but they rarely specify the player’s objective, the decisions that require reasoning, or the information that should be retained beyond the recent context. We

regions.label: text
regions.text: Raw gameplay videos provide rich visual and control experience, but they rarely specify the player’s objective, the decisions that require reasoning, or the information that should be retained beyond the recent context. We develop a scalable annotation pipeline that turns heterogeneous recordings into supervision for long-horizon task following, as shown in Figure 7 . Starting from tens of thousands of hours of raw gameplay collected across different sources, we filter invalid or misaligned recordings and balance coverage across gameplay scenarios. For SFT, we curate approximately 1K hours of gameplay trajectories. GPT-5.6-Luna [ 34 ] generates sparse action reasoning, task segments with instructions and scene descriptions, and task-state memories. We organize these annotations into three instruction levels: local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages. Hierarchical SFT Annotaion from Real HSR Trajectories

regions.label: text
regions.text: Data sources, filtering, and scenario balancing. We collect raw gameplay recordings with associated keyboard and mouse events from multiple sources. Within this collection, the HSR recording track contains roughly 68K sessions and 11K hours of video. Rather than annotating all available videos, we first select recordings with reliable visual and action supervision. We reject corrupted or duplicated sessions, missing or discontinuous frames, and trajectories whose video and action timestamps cannot be aligned consistently. We also remove invalid action traces, including mouse coordinates outside the valid screen or control bounds, malformed action states, and events that cross recording or interaction boundaries. Long inactive periods and recordings without meaningful interaction are filtered, while valid held inputs and task-related waiting periods are retained.

GPT-5.6-Luna identifies a sparse set of decision points, typically when the player selects or corrects a route, handles a new interaction prompt, changes objective, recovers from an unsuccessful attempt, or responds to a significant scene transition. Each Think annotation describes the observed outcome, the current decision, and an intended next action. Continuous movement, repeated controls, and minor camera corrections usually receive no separate reasoning target. Windows with neither meaningful input nor visual change can be skipped. regions.label: text
regions.text: After task segmentation, we reuse the clip images and cleaned task segments in a second conversational turn to generate memory annotations. The model returns all summaries for the clip in one response, typically one per 16-second window. Each summary briefly describes, in the first person, the cumulative accomplishments and outcomes within the clip up to the window end. A final window shorter than 8 seconds is merged into the preceding window. Postprocessing associates each summary with the active task instruction and the latest image frame at or before the window end.

regions.text: Training follows three stages while preserving the model architecture and action representation. CPT learns transferable control with key remapping and repeat-aware loss decay. SFT introduces multi-level task supervision, sparse reasoning, and cross-context memory. TA-GRPO then improves long-horizon behavior through online interaction, using environment-verifiable rewards and temporal credit assignment. Gameplay trajectories are sampled at 5 Hz, with six action blocks per step providing approximately 30 Hz control and a local visual history of 20 frames.

We extend Verl [ 44 ] into a unified training and evaluation framework, using Streaming-vLLM for interactive evaluation and online RL rollouts. A sharded inference service pool backed by 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs serves 32 parallel game environments. Each RL iteration collects 128 rollouts in groups of 8, with environment-verifiable rewards and no learned process reward model. Updated policy weights are synchronized across the service pool before the next rollout collection, keeping policy versions aligned throughout online training. Streaming-vLLM also supports dense and MoE backbones on NVIDIA A800 and H200 GPUs. Further configuration details are provided in Table 15 and Appendix F.1 .

regions.text: The controlled scaling study spans 120 CPT configurations and approximately 45K H200 GPU-hours. Shorter training budgets are derived from shared Warmup-Stable-Decay trajectories with separate final decay phases. For the subsequent Gamer training stages, CPT uses a distributed H200 cluster, SFT uses a distributed A800 cluster, and online RL uses Megatron/MCore with BF16 optimization. Real-time rollouts run in parallel game environments served by a sharded Streaming-vLLM pool backed by 64 H200 GPUs. The pool receives synchronized policy checkpoints between rollout iterations, enabling consistent interaction data collection as training progresses. More details of training configurations and stage-specific settings are summarized in Table 15 .

More details of training configurations and stage-specific settings are summarized in Table 15 .

regions.text: 7.3 Automated RL Environment A shared infrastructure for learning, evaluation, and testing. Many existing game-RL benchmarks run as lightweight, self-contained simulators that can be reset cheaply and queried directly for rewards. Modern commercial games present a substantially harder setting. In particular, Honkai: Star Rail depends on a full game client, supporting online services, GPU-accelerated rendering, and complex game-state dependencies. Reproducing its native mechanics in a lightweight simulator would change the interaction setting, while simply replicating game clients does not provide controlled initialization or objective verification. These challenges extend beyond online RL to large-scale automated evaluation and gameplay testing, where hundreds of executions must start from comparable states and be judged against consistent success criteria. We therefore build a dedicated, engine-instrumented sandbox that makes this resource-intensive game reproducible, verifiable, and scalable without changing the agent’s visual-control interface. Game-native rules as a unified source of feedback. We adapt the game engine to expose task-relevant state transitions and completion conditions to the environment backend. The resulting rule-based verifiers serve three complementary purposes. During online RL, they provide environment-verifiable rewards for TA-GRPO without a learned process reward model. During evaluation, they measure task completion objectively across models and policy checkpoints. For automated gameplay testing, the same checks provide reproducible pass/fail criteria for interactions and quest progression. This shared verification layer avoids relying on subjective assessments of generated text or inferring complex task outcomes from individual screenshots. GM-controlled initialization and reproducible execution. We integrate game-master (GM) commands to prepare predefined task states and restore the corresponding conditions before an episode. Each task pairs an initialization procedure with a target state, a completion check, and a termination rule. This allows the same objective to be executed repeatedly for policy optimization, fair comparison, and systematic testing of game behaviors. regions.label: text
regions.text: Our evaluation examines three complementary questions. First, we summarize the study in GameScaling, which evaluates 120 CPT configurations to characterize the effects of model scale, gameplay budget, and data composition. We then assess the executable cross-game performance of CPT policies built on Dense and MoE backbones. Next, we evaluate the separately trained HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT and its SFT and RL successors on HSR side quests and minigames, separating broad interaction skills from long-horizon task execution. Finally, we test whether real-time rollout collection supports online learning and whether Streaming-vLLM delivers the accuracy and latency needed for sustained interaction. regions.label: text
regions.text: 8.1 Evaluation Setup Public game benchmarks. We evaluate game-control policies on MCU [ 68 ], ViZDoom [ 56 ], OmniGameArena [ 25 ], and GameWorld [ 36 ]. These benchmarks vary in how far they differ from the gameplay data used for CPT. Specifically, MCU and ViZDoom evaluate game domains represented during CPT and primarily measure control learning within training-covered environments. OmniGameArena evaluates transfer to unseen three dimensional games with related interaction semantics. GameWorld provides a more distant cross-game transfer setting with larger shifts in visual appearance, control mechanics, and task structure. We follow the task definitions, environment settings, and native scoring protocols of the corresponding benchmarks. Each benchmark retains its original evaluation metric. We distinguish idealized time-paused (TP) evaluation from real-time (RT) interaction. TP pauses the environment during model inference, whereas RT allows the game to continue advancing. In the public game comparison, we report the RT score as the main value and its signed difference from TP (RT TP) in parentheses. − Across game evaluations, we use the same set of strong multimodal baselines wherever they support the required visual-control interface. These include GPT-6.1-Sol [ 35 ], Gemini-3.8-Flash [ 13 ], GPT-5.6-Sol [ 34 ], GPT-5.6-Luna [ 34 ], Claude-Opus-5.0 [ 1 ], GLM-5.3-Flash [ 61 ], and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision [ 10 ]. The same baseline pool is reused in the Honkai: Star Rail side-quest and minigame evaluations to provide a consistent comparison across control, instruction following, and gameplay generalization.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Specifically, MCU and ViZDoom evaluate game domains represented during CPT and primarily measure control learning within training-covered environments. OmniGameArena evaluates transfer to unseen three dimensional games with related interaction semantics. GameWorld provides a more distant cross-game transfer setting with larger shifts in visual appearance, control mechanics, and task structure. We follow the task definitions, environment settings, and native scoring protocols of the corresponding benchmarks. Each benchmark retains its original evaluation metric. We distinguish idealized time-paused (TP) evaluation from real-time (RT) interaction. TP pauses the environment during model inference, whereas RT allows the game to continue advancing. In the public game comparison, we report the RT score as the main value and its signed difference from TP (RT TP) in parentheses. − Across game evaluations, we use the same set of strong multimodal baselines wherever they support the required visual-control interface. These include GPT-6.1-Sol [ 35 ], Gemini-3.8-Flash [ 13 ], GPT-5.6-Sol [ 34 ], GPT-5.6-Luna [ 34 ], Claude-Opus-5.0 [ 1 ], GLM-5.3-Flash [ 61 ], and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision [ 10 ]. The same baseline pool is reused in the Honkai: Star Rail side-quest and minigame evaluations to provide a consistent comparison across control, instruction following, and gameplay generalization.

regions.text: Honkai: Star Rail evaluation suite. We construct two complementary evaluation sets in Honkai: Star Rail, comprising side quests and minigame tasks held out from training (Figure 9 ). Although the final CPT model has seen other gameplay from the same game, it has not been trained on these evaluation tasks or their target completions. This setting tests generalization to new tasks within a familiar game, rather than zero-shot transfer to an unseen game. The first set contains two long-horizon side quests that test sustained progress on complex instructions. Each quest may combine navigation, dialogue, combat, puzzles, and item interactions across several intermediate objectives. To finish a quest, the agent must remember quest information, track subgoal progress, and use that task state to guide low-level control. regions.label: text
regions.text: Each quest has a fixed initial state, task objective, milestone sequence, verifier, and termination condition. We report accuracy as the fraction of evaluated task executions that succeed, both overall and for each interaction type. The milestone inventory covers navigation, dialogue, combat, UI interaction, and, where applicable, puzzle solving. These rates measure verified progress across task executions rather than uninterrupted end-to-end quest completion. The complete milestones, types, and budgets are given in Appendix D .

regions.text: The second subset contains 40 instances across 7 minigame types, covering pattern composition, logical reasoning, spatial reasoning, temporal planning, and timing-sensitive control. Each type contains between one and sixteen evaluated instances. Figure 10 illustrates the minigame mechanics and instance distribution. We report the success rates for each type and compute overall accuracy as the unweighted mean of the seven type-level rates. Each type therefore contributes equally, regardless of its number of instances. Per-instance evaluation and taxonomy are described in Appendix D .

regions.label: text
regions.text: Figure 10 Overview of the minigame benchmark in the Honkai: Star Rail evaluation suite. The benchmark contains 40 task instances across seven game types. The left panel shows representative gameplay examples, instance counts, and mechanics. The upper-right chart shows the number of instances per type, while the lower-right chart groups minigames by four descriptive primary capability tags, with instance totals in parentheses. Each minigame type is assigned one primary tag for counting and may require additional abilities. Screenshots illustrate game types and are not necessarily drawn from the evaluated instances.

regions.text: As summarized in Table 3 , the study comprises 4 6 5 = 120 configurations spanning Qwen3.5 backbone × × sizes, gameplay budgets, and data mixtures. All other training settings are held fixed. Across configurations, gameplay trajectories account for 85% of training tokens, while the remaining 15% come from a fixed pool of general multimodal data. The remaining gameplay data in S2–S5 are sampled from the same multi-game pool.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Larger models learn more efficiently early in training, but their gains still depend on data composition. Under single-game training, stronger adaptation to Minecraft can coincide with degraded performance on other games. Multi-game mixtures alleviate this effect. For distant unseen games, validation loss typically improves during early interface adaptation and then plateaus or increases even while training loss continues to decrease. These observations motivate considering model capacity, interaction budget, and target-game coverage jointly.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Evaluation results on game benchmarks complement the validation-loss analysis with executable gameplay outcomes. As shown in Figure 14 , additional CPT experience generally improves performance in training covered and behaviorally related environments, particularly at smaller model scales. The comparison across S1-S5 also shows why the amount of gameplay alone is an incomplete description of the training signal. Mixtures that expose the model to multiple interaction patterns provide broader coverage than single-game training and support transfer to related environments. For Gamer, these findings motivate scaling game diversity alongside data volume rather than treating all recorded gameplay hours as equally informative for every target game.

regions.label: text
regions.text: While the controlled GameScaling study reveals how model size and gameplay data affect CPT, an important question remains: whether CPT can translate general-purpose visual understanding into executable control across diverse games. Unlike static visual reasoning, gameplay requires the agent to continuously interpret observations, execute precise actions, and adapt to evolving environments. We therefore evaluate whether CPT-trained policies can achieve effective real-time control across different games and backbone architectures. Table 5 compares two CPT checkpoints, initialized from Qwen3-VL-8B Dense and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE, with general-purpose multimodal baselines on four public game benchmarks. We report real-time (RT) scores as the primary results, together with their signed differences from time-paused (TP) evaluation.

regions.text: CPT supports effective cross-game control across Dense and MoE backbones. The Qwen3-VL-8B CPT policy achieves an average real-time score of 29.5, while the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE CPT policy reaches 31.5.

regions.label: text
regions.text: CPT supports effective cross-game control across Dense and MoE backbones. The Qwen3-VL-8B CPT policy achieves an average real-time score of 29.5, while the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE CPT policy reaches 31.5. Both exceed the strongest listed general-purpose baseline. The difference is especially clear on MCU, where the two CPT policies score 47.7 and 65.3, respectively. Their results also show complementary strengths across games. The 8B Dense policy achieves 21.9 on OmniGameArena and 34.0 on GameWorld, while the MoE policy performs particularly strongly on MCU. These results extend the scaling analysis from action prediction and validation loss to executable gameplay, and show that the CPT approach is applicable to both Dense and MoE model architectures.

regions.text: 8.3 Long-Horizon Instruction Following in Side Quests The two side quests require the agent to carry out multi-stage tasks while retaining information from earlier interactions. Table 6 reports verified task-execution success rates on Gamer. SFT substantially improves long-horizon task execution. On Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) , overall accuracy increases from 0.0% for Qwen3-VL-8B to 34.4% after HSR-augmented CPT and 72.2% after SFT. On Bestial Ferocity , the corresponding scores are 13.9%, 47.9%, and 69.1%. Thus, SFT adds 37.8 and 21.2 percentage points over the respective CPT checkpoints. The improvement is visible across distinct interaction types. For example, navigation rises from 14.3% to 47.6% on the first quest, while dialogue increases from 70.8% to 97.9% on the second. These outcomes are consistent with the objective of multi-level instruction tuning, which trains the same action policy to follow goals that span local operations, intermediate subgoals, and longer task sequences. Both quests involve repeated scene transitions, UI interactions, and changes in objectives. To make progress, the agent must retain relevant information from earlier interactions and use it to decide what to do next. SFT improves performance on held-out tasks, suggesting that task-conditioned reasoning and memory can support this behavior in a familiar game, even when the specific evaluation objectives were excluded from training. Online RL further strengthens long-horizon execution. We perform online RL on the basis of the SFT checkpoint. Relative to its SFT initialization, TA-GRPO improves overall task-execution accuracy from 72.2% to 80.0% on Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) and from 69.1% to 83.6% on Bestial Ferocity . These correspond to gains of 7.8 and 14.5 percentage points , respectively. Navigation accuracy rises from 47.6% to 69.1% on the first quest and from 55.2% to 80.2% on the second. On Bestial Ferocity , dialogue reaches 100% after RL. These results suggest that verified interaction feedback helps refine the policy’s ability to advance toward task goals over extended trajectories. The gains across both side quests highlight the complementary roles of instruction supervision and online policy optimization. SFT provides task-conditioned decisions and memory, while RL allows the policy to learn from the consequences of its own actions under game-native verification. Importantly, these improvements are obtained without changing the underlying action interface or model architecture. Appendix E provides

regions.label: footer
regions.text: 8.4 Instruction Generalization across Diverse Minigames

regions.label: footer
regions.text: The minigame suite emphasizes instruction following across different gameplay mechanics. This broader coverage is important because the tasks require different combinations of spatial reasoning, rule interpretation, visual matching, and device-level interaction rather than a single repeated control routine. Table 7 reports success for each of the seven types and their unweighted macro-average. Instruction tuning broadens success across distinct minigame mechanics. The seven-type macro-average increases from 3.2% for the base Qwen3-VL-8B to 15.0% for Gamer-CPT and 39.2% for Gamer-SFT, a further gain of 24.2 percentage points after instruction tuning. SFT reaches 76.2% on Janus’s Hidden Passage, 52.4% on Janus’s Maze, and 50.0% on Navigation Compass. It also obtains non-zero mean success in all seven types, compared with three for the base model. The CPT checkpoint already improves the macro-average, providing a useful foundation for responding to gameplay observations and actions. SFT then connects these control capabilities to task-specific goals, which is reflected in improvements across puzzles with different interfaces and completion rules. The evaluation tasks are held out from training, so the comparison measures generalization to new instances and objectives within HSR. Online RL further improves performance across diverse mechanics. Following SFT, Gamer-RL raises the seven-type macro-average from 39.2% to 49.7% , an additional gain of 10.5 percentage points . The improvement is particularly pronounced on Navigation Compass, where accuracy increases from 50.0% to 95.8%. RL also improves Magflow Link from 40.0% to 53.3%, Hexanexus from 11.1% to 33.3% and Janus’s Hidden Passage from 76.2% to 81.0%, with additional gains on Abacus Circuitry and Golden Scapegoat. These results extend the benefits of online policy optimization beyond long-horizon quests to tasks involving diverse rules and interaction patterns. Together, the CPT, SFT, and RL stages progressively improve the model’s ability to interpret instructions and execute actions across different game mechanics. To prevent game types with more tasks from dominating the aggregate, the overall metric first averages attempts within each task and then gives each of the seven types equal weight. This makes the reported improvement a measure of breadth across mechanics rather than only the most frequent minigame.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Instruction tuning broadens success across distinct minigame mechanics. The seven-type macro-average increases from 3.2% for the base Qwen3-VL-8B to 15.0% for Gamer-CPT and 39.2% for Gamer-SFT, a further gain of 24.2 percentage points after instruction tuning. SFT reaches 76.2% on Janus’s Hidden Passage, 52.4% on Janus’s Maze, and 50.0% on Navigation Compass. It also obtains non-zero mean success in all seven types, compared with three for the base model. The CPT checkpoint already improves the macro-average, providing a useful foundation for responding to gameplay observations and actions. SFT then connects these control capabilities to task-specific goals, which is reflected in improvements across puzzles with different interfaces and completion rules. The evaluation tasks are held out from training, so the comparison measures generalization to new instances and objectives within HSR.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Online RL further improves performance across diverse mechanics. Following SFT, Gamer-RL raises the seven-type macro-average from 39.2% to 49.7% , an additional gain of 10.5 percentage points . The improvement is particularly pronounced on Navigation Compass, where accuracy increases from 50.0% to 95.8%. RL also improves Magflow Link from 40.0% to 53.3%, Hexanexus from 11.1% to 33.3% and Janus’s Hidden Passage from 76.2% to 81.0%, with additional gains on Abacus Circuitry and Golden Scapegoat. These results extend the benefits of online policy optimization beyond long-horizon quests to tasks involving diverse rules and interaction patterns. Together, the CPT, SFT, and RL stages progressively improve the model’s ability to interpret instructions and execute actions across different game mechanics.

regions.text: Real-time interaction is critical for online RL in modern games. Unlike lightweight simulators, modern games involve continuously evolving environments, complex gameplay mechanics, and state-dependent interactions.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Real-time interaction is critical for online RL in modern games. Unlike lightweight simulators, modern games involve continuously evolving environments, complex gameplay mechanics, and state-dependent interactions. In this setting, inference latency affects not only the responsiveness of the deployed agent but also the quality and efficiency of online policy learning. Delayed control can cause subsequent actions to operate on outdated observations, making it harder to obtain timely feedback from the environment. We therefore examine the effect of rollout frequency on RL training, comparing real-time Streaming-vLLM against standard vLLM rollouts. The game continues to advance under both settings.

regions.text: Timely control supports more effective online policy learning. As shown in Figure 11 , real-time Streaming vLLM consistently demonstrates more favorable learning dynamics than the standard vLLM setting across eight navigation tasks. First, real-time rollouts achieve higher rewards from the early stages of training. Timely observation and action execution reduce accumulated interaction errors, allowing the agent to reach intended states more reliably and obtain informative reward feedback more efficiently. Second, real-time training achieves higher reward levels, particularly on tasks involving time-sensitive navigation and interactions, where delayed control can prevent the agent from completing the required action sequences. More importantly, several low-FPS runs exhibit reward collapse in the later stages of training. This behavior suggests that accumulated execution errors can introduce increasingly biased trajectories into online optimization, undermining subsequent policy updates and training stability. In contrast, real-time interaction maintains more reliable environment feedback and supports sustained policy improvement. regions.title: Timely control supports more effective online policy learning. As shown in Figure 11 , real-time Streaming vLLM consistently demonstrates more favorable learning dynamics than the standard vLLM setting across eight navigation tasks. regions.text: Streaming video benchmarks. In addition to low latency, an inference engine must preserve the model’s ability to understand and respond to continuously arriving visual input. To verify the inference accuracy of our Streaming-vLLM, we further evaluate streaming inference on StreamingBench [ 24 ] and OVO-Bench [ 33 ]. For StreamingBench, we use the Real-Time Visual Understanding subset. OVO-Bench evaluates current-event understanding through Real , retrieval of earlier information through Backward , and delayed response after sufficient evidence through Forward .

regions.text: Streaming-vLLM preserves visual understanding while reducing inference latency. Table 8 presents matched backbone comparisons on two complementary streaming benchmarks. With Qwen3-VL-8B, Streaming-vLLM scores 83.29 on StreamingBench and 62.3 on OVO-Bench, reducing query latency from 0.53 to 0.08 s relative to DSCache. With Qwen3.5-9B, it reaches 83.77 and 60.9, respectively, while latency falls from 1.56 to 0.16 s. The OVO-Bench improvements appear in its Real, Backward, and Forward subsets, suggesting that the retained context remains useful for both incoming visual evidence and information from earlier video frames.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Gamer learns to control diverse and complex games through a shared keyboard-and-mouse interface. It combines large-scale continued pre-training, task-conditioned supervised fine-tuning, and temporal-aware reinforcement learning to learn transferable control, long-horizon reasoning, and persistent memory. Streaming vLLM supports both training and deployment, enabling real-time interaction and efficient online rollouts while reducing latency-induced bias in reinforcement learning. At inference time, Gamer acts through visual observations and device-level controls without privileged game state or game-engine modifications. Environment-side task verification is used separately to provide online RL rewards. These capabilities could effectively reduce development costs through automated testing, faster game iteration, and new gameplay mechanics. By supporting real-time interaction without game-specific infrastructure, Gamer offers a basis for agents that learn and improve across complex 3D games and other interactive environments.

regions.text: Several main directions remain for extending Gamer’s scope and accessibility. First, our evaluation covers a selected set of environments and task structures. The shared observation-action interface provides a basis for extending joint post-training and systematic evaluation to broader interactive settings. Our preliminary results suggest the potential for improving performance and generalization by scaling relevant gameplay data across a broader range of environments. These benefits depend on the coverage and composition of the training experience.

regions.text: Third, although Gamer improves the trade-off between response latency and task performance in the evaluated settings, reasoning capability may remain a bottleneck in environments that demand deeper deliberation. regions.text: Recent work further targets generalization across tasks and worlds. Gato [ 42 ] and SIMA [ 41 ] study shared policies across heterogeneous environments, while Game-TARS [ 55 ] and Lumine [ 45 ] combine reasoning, memory, and native keyboard–mouse control for extended gameplay. GameHorizon [ 51 ] introduces temporal hierarchy into gameplay supervision, while OmniJARVIS [ 53 ] and Lumine [ 45 ] combine reasoning, memory, and staged training. We train the policy with supervision at the operation, subgoal, and task levels, and retain compact task summaries across context boundaries.

We optimize finite trajectory segments linked by compressed memory, updating task-state maintenance and executable behavior together. regions.label: text
regions.text: The fixed non-Minecraft pool contains 124 source-stream labels mapping to 79 canonical game labels. The three validation distributions separate Minecraft held-out clips, training-covered game clips, and title-disjoint unseen-game clips. The latter is game-balanced, with 28 unseen titles and 160 clips per title (4,480 clips in total). Grouping by source recording and removing title aliases limit overlap between training and validation. These splits distinguish transfer of the action interface from gains limited to games in the training mixture.

regions.text: Block-wise holdout evaluation. To evaluate predictive performance beyond the configurations used for fitting, we remove complete blocks of model sizes, data budgets, or game mixtures. For each holdout setting, the scaling relation is refit using the remaining configurations, and RMSE is computed only over the held-out block. Mixture prediction is more sensitive to the availability of nearby compositions, particularly for Minecraft when S4 is held out.

regions.text: B.4 Scaling Robustness and Predictive Uncertainty

regions.label: text
regions.text: B.4 Scaling Robustness and Predictive Uncertainty

regions.label: text
regions.text: The composition-aware relation explains both differences among mixtures and their different slopes with respect to gameplay hours. An equally parameterized categorical-offset alternative cannot predict a held-out mixture and yields higher training-grid errors: Minecraft RMSE 0.0044 versus 0.0020 and in-corpus RMSE 0.0035 versus 0.0012. By contrast, distant unseen-game losses generally rise after the early interface phase, and their within-mixture scaling fit is weak. We therefore interpret the fitted relation as an empirical description of the measured in-corpus data regime rather than a universal law for unseen environments. Figure 15 and Table 12 demonstrate the fit’s accuracy and limitations.

regions.title: Figure 16 Frontier-model progress on four public game benchmarks. Scores are plotted against model release date under time-paused evaluation. Circles indicate the GPT series, squares the Qwen series, and stars the GameScaling-S3 checkpoints at 1,600 gameplay hours (marked GS in the original plot). These results are from the controlled scaling study, not the HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT model. The comparison shows gains from gameplay adaptation alongside the contribution of general backbone capabilities, particularly on distant worlds.

regions.text: FSM grammar coverage. The SM90 fast FSM recognizes the boundaries <think> , </think> , <|action_- start|> , and <|action_end|> . It can draft the end of an empty reasoning span or the beginning of an action packet after a finished reasoning span. Within the XYZ mouse-coordinate fields, the FSM drafts formatting tokens following numerical values, not the coordinate values themselves. In the six subsequent key groups, it drafts predictable delimiters, blank-key templates, and the action terminator. Candidate tokens are proposed opportunistically when the current grammar state supports them.

regions.text: Target-model verification. The drafts are checked by the target model before being committed. A candidate prefix is accepted only where each drafted token equals the token that target-model verification selects at the

regions.label: text
regions.text: Target-model verification. The drafts are checked by the target model before being committed. A candidate prefix is accepted only where each drafted token equals the token that target-model verification selects at the corresponding position under the active sampling rule (greedy argmax or temperature sampling); rejected suffixes and their speculative cache states are discarded. Throughout generation, the FSM simultaneously enforces grammar-level constrained decoding and speculative drafting: at every decoding and verification position, it restricts token selection to valid protocol transitions via state-dependent vocabulary bitmasks in the fused sampler—including for tokenizers whose action delimiters span multiple subword pieces—while proposing predictable structural continuations as drafts for parallel target-model verification, without replacing the policy’s semantic action decisions over coordinate values or valid key combinations.

regions.text: Both updated components are computed from the original pair before being written back to the cache. The implementation follows the component-pair layout used by the underlying model and applies the corresponding update independently to all dimensions participating in RoPE. Tokens whose logical positions remain unchanged have ∆ p = 0 and therefore require no modification. The update is performed in place on the retained key cache. No unrotated key representation is stored, and the value cache is left unchanged. For RoPE variants with multiple positional axes, the same correction is applied independently to the component groups associated with each axis. This update corrects only the rotary positional phase. As discussed in Sec. 5.1 , retained KV states continue to follow the stateful streaming semantics of Streaming-vLLM rather than being reconstructed through full re-encoding after memory compaction.

regions.text: C.4 Latency Composition and Control-Rate Interpretation The end-to-end request time comprises vision encoding, context processing, action generation, and runtime overhead. In the figure, Ampere denotes NVIDIA A800, and Hopper denotes NVIDIA H200. Figure 19 compares these components across model architectures, hardware generations, parallel settings, and numerical precision. The system ablation reports step rate (SR), the reciprocal of end-to-end request latency, and a theoretical control rate (CR) obtained by multiplying SR by the six low-level blocks in each action packet. CR is a latency-derived upper bound, not a direct measurement of the client execution cadence. The latter uses approximately 33 ms per block (30 Hz) when actions arrive in time.

regions.text: C.4 Latency Composition and Control-Rate Interpretation The end-to-end request time comprises vision encoding, context processing, action generation, and runtime overhead. In the figure, Ampere denotes NVIDIA A800, and Hopper denotes NVIDIA H200. Figure 19 compares these components across model architectures, hardware generations, parallel settings, and numerical precision. The system ablation reports step rate (SR), the reciprocal of end-to-end request latency, and a theoretical control rate (CR) obtained by multiplying SR by the six low-level blocks in each action packet. CR is a latency-derived upper bound, not a direct measurement of the client execution cadence. The latter uses approximately 33 ms per block (30 Hz) when actions arrive in time.

regions.text: Figure 19 Cross-backbone request latency on NVIDIA A800 (Ampere) and H200 (Hopper). The existing sweep compares Qwen3-VL-8B (Dense) and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (MoE) across tensor-parallel degrees and BF16 or W8A8 execution. Stacked values separate vision processing, context (prefill), generation (decode), and remaining overhead, measured as mean request latency. These results characterize representative hardware and backbone coverage rather than all supported model sizes. The theoretical control rate in Table 9 is derived from request time, not measured at the client.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Honkai: Star Rail provides a useful setting for studying generalist game agents because its complexity comes from combining familiar interactions across a large, varied world, rather than from a single difficult mechanic. Figure 20 brings together 171 floor maps from 85 areas across the game’s major worlds. The maps range from compact rooms and branching corridors to large open layouts, interconnected structures, and multi-floor environments. Even when presented at a common coordinate scale, their differences are apparent. An agent cannot assume that a route learned in one area will work in another. It must adjust to new geometry, identify transitions between areas or floors, and preserve its destination as the scene changes.

regions.label: number
regions.text: The many point icons also reveal how exploration and task execution are interleaved. Individual areas contain resources and other points of interest alongside locations relevant to progression and interaction. A route can pass several optional objects before reaching the target, and the shortest visible path need not be a feasible sequence of game actions. The red paths in Figure 20 are schematic exploration routes , not gameplay-verified optimal solutions. They illustrate the need to plan through branching spaces, but do not establish that any particular route is the fastest or most reliable. The annotated maps are provided only to describe the environment and are not given to the evaluated agents as observations or privileged navigation input.

regions.label: number
regions.text: Accessible gameplay does not imply easy autonomous control. For a human player, quest objectives, map markers, and familiar interaction prompts make many individual steps understandable. A vision-language action agent receives only the rendered screen and must turn this guidance into timed keyboard and mouse inputs. It must recognize where it is, distinguish relevant objects from nearby distractions, navigate while the camera and scene change, and determine when an interaction has actually completed. Longer tasks add another difficulty: navigation, dialogue, UI manipulation, combat, and local puzzles may appear within the same quest. Failure at one step can invalidate a later plan, and an agent must remember earlier progress even after those observations leave its active context. The challenge is therefore not simply to play any one minigame, but to coordinate heterogeneous skills over time.

regions.label: number
regions.text: This combination makes the game useful for both research and practical evaluation. Short interactive challenges probe whether a policy can adapt to different local rules, while side quests test whether those skills support sustained, instruction-conditioned progress. The same interface also reflects conditions faced by automated game testing: new content introduces routes, objects, objectives, and mechanics that cannot all be anticipated by hand-written scripts. A generalist agent able to execute these tasks through screen observations and device-level actions could support exploration, quest verification, and regression testing without modifications to the game engine. These are potential applications , not deployment benefits measured by the map itself.

The same interface also reflects conditions faced by automated game testing: new content introduces routes, objects, objectives, and mechanics that cannot all be anticipated by hand-written scripts. A generalist agent able to execute these tasks through screen observations and device-level actions could support exploration, quest verification, and regression testing without modifications to the game engine. These are potential applications , not deployment benefits measured by the map itself.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Exploration is only one part of Honkai: Star Rail . Combat adds a different decision-making problem within the same game interface. The game uses turn-based encounters, but choosing an action still depends on information that changes throughout the fight. As shown in Figure 21 , the combat screen combines the action-order queue with character HP, enemy Toughness, team status, skill points, and available abilities. The action-order display and Action Value indicate when combatants will act, while the Toughness system creates opportunities for Weakness Break. The agent must use these cues together, rather than treating each turn as an isolated image-to-action decision.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Combat decisions involve coupled constraints over multiple turns. Attacking a vulnerable target may advance a Weakness Break, but the agent must also consider the available skill points, the health and status of its team, and which combatant acts next. Character roles introduce further variation. The Paths shown in Figure 21 span single-target and multi-target damage, buffs and debuffs, protection and healing, summons, and other specialized combat effects. A useful action can therefore depend on the team composition and on how one character’s choice changes the options available to others. Although human players can read these cues from a familiar interface, an autonomous policy must recognize them visually, choose a suitable action, and issue the corresponding executable inputs.

regions.label: text
regions.text: We compute accuracy by first averaging the success outcomes of valid attempts for each task, then averaging task scores within each game type, and finally taking an unweighted mean over the seven type-level scores. Unlike an any-success-at-three metric, this score retains fractional success rates when a task succeeds in only a subset of its attempts. The seven-type macro-average prevents categories with more tasks from dominating the result.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Extended Main-Story Evaluation. Beyond side quests and minigames, we further evaluate Gamer on the main

regions.label: text
regions.text: Extended Main-Story Evaluation. Beyond side quests and minigames, we further evaluate Gamer on the main storyline of Honkai: Star Rail, covering five major story arcs with 19 quest chains and 160 main-story mission entries. Across approximately 50 hours of gameplay evaluation, our model operates autonomously for over 95% of the total evaluation time, demonstrating sustained gameplay proficiency across diverse environments, complex interactions, and long sequences of evolving objectives. This result highlights the potential of generalist game agents to support extended autonomous gameplay beyond isolated benchmark tasks. With further reinforcement learning and model scaling, generalist game agents could serve as foundational tools for large-scale automated evaluation and testing of large modern games.

regions.title: Figure 23 Navigation across RL checkpoints on a training task (Reach Pom-Pom). Each row shows one representative rollout with twelve temporally ordered observations, actions, and translated reasoning excerpts. Task successes reports successful attempts out of 16 for each checkpoint: 3, 5, 14, 13, 15, and 15 for CP 0-50, respectively. Red boxes mark scene details or interaction prompts, and blue shading marks reasoning excerpts. The illustrated CP 0 and CP 10 attempts time out, while CP 20-50 reach the target and complete the interaction. Frame counts and completion times describe only the displayed rollout.

regions.text: Across both cases, the increase in successful attempts is accompanied by more goal-directed behavior in the illustrated trajectories. Later policies more consistently select routes around obstacles, avoid unrelated interactions, and carry through to the final task-verifying action rather than stopping near the target location. The 16-attempt counts quantify the change in completion reliability, while the examples help interpret what that improvement looks like during execution. Together with the held-out side-quest results, they illustrate how online training can strengthen navigation and sustained goal pursuit.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Evaluation separation. Training/validation/test splits are defined at the complete recording or task-source level before extracting overlapping action windows or multi-level examples. For interaction benchmarks, time-paused (TP) evaluation freezes the simulated environment during policy inference, whereas real-time (RT) evaluation lets the environment advance. These settings use the same action serialization but different timing semantics. Real-time performance comparisons should therefore report both the serving configuration and environment timing rather than treating model size or score as a proxy for latency.

regions.label: text
regions.text: Rollout and evaluation protocol. Interactive inference produces six keyboard-mouse control blocks from the current visual observation, task instruction, and memory context. The client executes these blocks while the environment continues to advance. Online RL runs across 32 parallel game environments served by a sharded Streaming-vLLM pool with 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each iteration gathers 128 rollouts in groups of eight from the active navigation or puzzle task pool. Two disjoint rollout subsets support the policy updates, and environment task verification provides rewards without a learned process reward model. SFT and RL evaluations use matched task initializations, milestone verifiers, action semantics, and inference settings as described in Sec. 8.3 .

Inference uses BF16 with a maximum generation length of 512 tokens and temperature 0.9. The game screenshots are captured at 1280 720 and resized to 854 480 for model input. TA-GRPO uses 20-turn segments and temporal factor β = 0 . 9 × . These settings, together with × the checkpoint and service synchronization protocol, specify the interaction conditions used in the reported experiments.

regions.title: Figure 19 Cross-backbone request latency on NVIDIA A800 (Ampere) and H200 (Hopper). The existing sweep compares Qwen3-VL-8B (Dense) and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (MoE) across tensor-parallel degrees and BF16 or W8A8 execution. Stacked values separate vision processing, context (prefill), generation (decode), and remaining overhead, measured as mean request latency. These results characterize representative hardware and backbone coverage rather than all supported model sizes. The theoretical control rate in Table 9 is derived from request time, not measured at the client.
